title: Holy days and the saints' calendar
hookLine: a few great feasts are kept like Sundays (the list varies by country)
tomorrow: Camp 3 close: a rule of life

cards: Open a Catholic calendar, the kind that hangs in a parish hall, and look at any square. There's a name in it. March 19, Joseph.

August 15, Mary taken up into heaven. November 1, all the saints at once. A random Tuesday in July still has a name: some bishop, some farmer's daughter, some martyr from a city you've never heard of.
Almost no day is empty. And a few squares carry a special mark, because on those days Catholics are asked to go to Mass, even on a Wednesday.

teach.h: MARKED DAYS: KEPT LIKE A SUNDAY.
teach.b: Those marked days are holy days of obligation.
Catholics are asked to go to Mass every Sunday, and on a handful of great feasts they're asked to do the same, whatever day of the week it falls on, and to rest from unnecessary work where they can.
The Church's general law lists ten, among them Christmas, the Epiphany, the Ascension, Mary the Mother of God, the Assumption, Saint Joseph, Peter and Paul, and All Saints.
But it lets each country's bishops trim the list or move a feast to the nearest Sunday. In the United States the list is shorter, and some are lifted when they fall right next to a weekend.
Ask a Catholic in Ireland or Italy and you'll get a different answer. Then there's everyone else on the calendar.
The Church keeps a general calendar of saints for the whole world, and a much longer book, the Roman Martyrology, lists saints and martyrs for every day of the year, often several on a single day.

teach.h: THE DAY THEY DIED: A BIRTHDAY.
teach.b: Here's the surprise: a saint's feast is usually kept on the day they died, not the day they were born.

The old Latin name for that day is dies natalis, birthday, because the Church thinks of it as their birthday into heaven. So every morning, somewhere, somebody is keeping a birthday for someone who died long ago.
Parishes are named for them. Children are named for them. And in some Catholic families, a name day is kept like a second birthday.

how: Catholics go to Mass on Sundays and on their country's holy days of obligation, such as Christmas and All Saints; many also follow the saints' calendar, keeping name days, the feasts of their parish's patron and their own patron saints.

games.why: that mark means a holy day of obligation. Catholics are asked to go to Mass and rest where they can, whatever day of the week it falls on.

practice: Think of today as already belonging to someone who lived a whole life and finished it; any Catholic calendar will tell you whose. Then think of someone you knew who has died, and the day that was theirs.
If you pray, ask today's saint to pray for you, or for them; if you don't, simply remember one life with gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Dies natalis. Latin for birthday, the day a saint died, kept as their birthday into heaven. Today's word.
